lead: A microwave integrated circuit (MIC) puts transmission lines, resistors, capacitors, inductors and transistors on one flat substrate, so a whole front end becomes a single printed board or a single chip. The hybrid version mounts ready-made transistors on a ceramic board. The monolithic version, the MMIC, builds every part inside one semiconductor wafer. Phones, radar modules, satellite receivers and 5G base stations use them because a compact, repeatable circuit with very short connections still works well above 1 GHz. This chapter covers the substrates, the on-chip components, the trade-offs and the packaging.
prereq: You need: microstrip and stripline from Unit 1, the wave view of a two-port from 4.1 S-parameters, and gain compression from the amplifier section of Unit 5.

sections.h3: Hybrid MIC: printed passives, mounted transistors

blocks.text: A microwave integrated circuit (MIC) is a complete microwave circuit built as a flat layered structure on one substrate. Every connection is a planar transmission line: microstrip, coplanar waveguide (CPW) or stripline. No long wires exist, so the circuit still behaves at frequencies where a wire would act as an inductor or an antenna.

In a hybrid MIC the substrate carries only the passive pattern: lines, couplers, filters and matching stubs. Transistors, diodes and chip capacitors are made separately and attached to that pattern by epoxy or solder, then joined with short bond wires. Hybrids are easy to modify and handle power well, but each bond wire adds roughly 1 nH per millimetre of inductance, which hurts at high frequency.

items: Alumina (Al₂O₃): εr ≈ 9.8, hard, cheap, good heat conduction; the workhorse for hybrid MICs. Common thicknesses are 0.25 mm and 0.635 mm.
Fused silica and quartz: εr ≈ 3.8, very low loss, used above about 20 GHz.
Semi-insulating GaAs: εr ≈ 12.9; used when the board must also carry monolithic devices.
LTCC (low-temperature co-fired ceramic): many dielectric layers, so 3-D passives and buried striplines fit inside one package.

blocks.text: Line geometry sets the impedance. For microstrip, the strip width w over substrate height h and permittivity εr fixes Z₀, and the guided wavelength is λg = λ₀/√εeff, where εeff lies between 1 and εr because part of the field travels in air. A microstrip patch antenna is just one more printed shape on the same substrate (see Unit 3). Thick-film paste printing is cheap but coarse; thin-film sputtering with photolithography gives fine lines and stable resistors.

sections.h3: MMIC: the whole circuit inside one wafer

blocks.text: A monolithic microwave integrated circuit (MMIC) forms every component — transistor, resistor, capacitor, inductor and line — in or on one semiconductor wafer. Nothing is bonded on. One process run yields thousands of identical circuits, and there are no bond-wire parasitics anywhere inside the chip.

items: Transistor: MESFET or HEMT on GaAs; HBT or RF-CMOS on silicon. Gain falls roughly 6 dB per octave, so a device with usable gain at 2 GHz has about 20 dB less gain at 20 GHz (about 3.3 octaves higher).
Resistor: a thin film (NiCr or TaN) or the active layer itself, set by its sheet resistance in Ω per square; value = sheet resistance × (length/width).
Capacitor: metal–insulator–metal (MIM) sandwich, C = εA/d with Si₃N₄ of thickness d ≈ 0.2 µm. Values are small, a few pF.
Inductor: a flat metal spiral; the best on-chip Q is about 10–20 because of series metal resistance and loss leaking into the substrate.
Airbridge: a thick plated metal strap jumping over the surface. It crosses other lines with little capacitance and carries current with low resistance.
Grow or implant the active layer on the semi-insulating wafer.
Isolate each device region by mesa etch or ion implantation.
Form ohmic contacts (AuGe/Ni/Au) and anneal; deposit the gate metal.
Deposit the dielectric, open contact windows, and build the MIM capacitors and thin-film resistors.
Sputter metal 1 for interconnects and spirals; plate the airbridge as metal 2, landing on metal 1.
Thin the wafer to about 100 µm, etch backside via holes down to ground, then dice and test.

blocks.text: GaAs is semi-insulating, with resistivity above 10⁷ Ω·cm, which is why a GaAs MMIC can carry low-loss lines straight on its own surface. InP serves circuits above 100 GHz. Silicon is the cheap high-volume choice, carrying RF-CMOS and SiGe HBT circuits such as the switch and front-end blocks inside a phone.

items: MMIC advantages: very small, repeatable from die to die, broadband because there are no bond wires, and cheap per piece in volume.
MMIC limits: low output power (a few watts at most, less on GaAs), a very expensive mask set and wafer run, no tuning after fabrication, low-Q passives, and yield loss across a large chip.
Hybrid advantages: tuneable by trimming, higher power, cheap tooling, quick to prototype.

blocks.text: Packaging is part of the design. The die is soldered or glued into a metal cavity, and connections leave by bond wires, by flip-chip bumps, or by a CPW launch into a coaxial connector. Wire bonds add series inductance, and a cavity that is a half-wave long at the operating frequency will resonate and spoil the match, so the lid height is chosen with care.

Passive measurement settles the process before any circuit is committed. A microstrip ring or half-wave resonator made on the same wafer gives the effective permittivity from its resonant frequency and the substrate loss from its Q, so εeff and loss tangent are known. A network analyser, as in 4.8, then measures S₂₁ and S₁₁ of the finished chip. Filters, couplers, dividers, low-noise amplifiers and power amplifiers built on these substrates are the subject of Unit 5.

figure.caption: Cross-section of a MMIC: the semi-insulating GaAs substrate carries the metal 1 interconnect, a passivation dielectric, and a plated airbridge across the top. Notice that the airbridge crosses the surface with air underneath it, which keeps its capacitance to the circuit small.

spec.aria: A five-layer stack, top to bottom: airbridge top metal, passivation dielectric, metal 1 interconnect, GaAs substrate and bottom ground metal.

examples.question: A MMIC power amplifier for a 5 GHz link has small-signal gain 10 dB and an output 1 dB compression point of 18 dBm. The input power is 8 dBm. Find (a) the output power if the amplifier were perfectly linear, (b) the actual output power, and (c) the compression in dB.
steps: Linear case: P_out = P_in + G = 8 dBm + 10 dB = 18 dBm. Adding a dB to a dBm gives a dBm.
The output 1 dB compression point is P1dB(out) = 18 dBm: the output at which the real curve sits 1 dB below the straight-line extension.
The linear value equals P1dB(out), so the device is exactly at the 1 dB compression point. The actual output is 1 dB below the linear value: 18 dBm − 1 dB = 17 dBm.
Compression = linear output − actual output = 18 dBm − 17 dBm = 1 dB. Subtracting dBm from dBm gives plain dB.
Gain under this drive = 17 dBm − 8 dBm = 9 dB, i.e. 1 dB below the small-signal gain of 10 dB.
examples.answer: Linear output 18 dBm, actual output 17 dBm, so the amplifier is compressed by 1 dB.
examples.check:
G_db = 10.0
P_in_dbm = 8.0
P1db_out_dbm = 18.0
P_lin = P_in_dbm + G_db
P_out = P1db_out_dbm - 1.0
comp = P_lin - P_out
print(P_lin)

traps: Calling every flat microwave board an MMIC. The test is whether the transistor is made inside the wafer or bonded onto it.
Treating on-chip spiral inductors as ideal. Their Q is only about 10–20, so a matching network built from them always loses some signal.
Using εr where εeff belongs. The microstrip guided wavelength uses εeff, which is smaller than εr because part of the field is in air.
Forgetting that bond wires and via holes are inductors, roughly 1 nH per millimetre of wire, which shifts the match at high frequency.
Mixing dB and dBm: dBm + dB = dBm, but dBm − dBm = dB. The compression figure is a plain dB number.

quiz.q: What does MMIC stand for, and which parts are no longer separate components?
quiz.a: Monolithic microwave integrated circuit. Transistors, resistors, capacitors, inductors and lines are all formed in or on one wafer; nothing is bonded on.

quiz.q: Name two substrate materials for MMICs and one property of each.
quiz.a: Semi-insulating GaAs, εr ≈ 12.9, good for HEMT and MESFET devices; InP, used above 100 GHz; silicon, cheap and high volume for RF-CMOS and SiGe.

quiz.q: Why is coplanar waveguide convenient for a MMIC that needs shunt elements?
quiz.a: The strip and both ground planes lie on the top surface, so a shunt element reaches ground through a short airbridge or via. No backside metal or through-wafer hole is needed for every ground connection.

quiz.q: A MMIC low-noise amplifier has gain 12 dB and output 1 dB compression point 5 dBm. The input is −7 dBm. Find the linear output power and the actual output power.
quiz.a: Linear output = −7 dBm + 12 dB = 5 dBm, which equals P1dB(out). At that point the actual output is 1 dB lower: 4 dBm, so the compression is 1 dB. Gain under drive = 4 dBm − (−7 dBm) = 11 dB, 1 dB below the small-signal 12 dB.

quiz.q: An on-chip spiral inductor of 2 nH has Q = 12 at 2 GHz. Find its series resistance and explain the cost.
quiz.a: R = ωL/Q = (2π × 2×10⁹ × 2×10⁻⁹)/12 = 25.13/12 ≈ 2.1 Ω. Signal current flows through this resistance, so the matching network loses power and the gain and noise figure both suffer.

quiz.q: Why does a MMIC usually handle less power than a hybrid MIC built with the same transistor type?
quiz.a: The die is small and thin, so heat has little material to spread into; the lines are narrow, so current density and metal migration set a limit; and the on-chip matching network adds loss. A hybrid spreads heat over a thicker ceramic and uses wider printed lines.

quiz.q: Why is a microstrip ring resonator tested on the wafer before circuits are finalised?
quiz.a: Its resonant frequency fixes the effective permittivity and its Q fixes the loss tangent, so the process line and substrate are characterised before design values are frozen.

beyond: Not for the exam. Gallium nitride MMICs on silicon carbide substrates now deliver several watts at X-band and above, which is why radar and satellite blocks have moved from tubes to chips. RF-SOI and RF-CMOS put the switch, low-noise amplifier and power amplifier of a phone on one silicon die, and heterogeneous integration stacks GaAs or GaN chiplets beside silicon. Useful searches are MMIC foundry process design kit, GaN MMIC power amplifier, and spiral inductor Q factor.
